questions.question: Which of the following instruments is used to measure the intensity of earthquakes?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Seismograph**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **seismograph**, also known as a **seismometer**, is an instrument designed to detect and record **seismic waves** produced by **earthquakes**, volcanic eruptions, or explosions.
 
• The primary **function** of the device is to record the **ground motion** over a period of **time**. It works on the principle of **inertia**, where a heavy mass remains stationary while the frame moves with the vibrating earth.
 
• The output produced by this instrument is a graph called a **seismogram**, which **geologists** and **seismologists** use to determine the **magnitude**, **depth**, and **location** of the earthquake's **epicenter**.
 
• Modern **seismographs** are highly sensitive **electronic** devices that can detect **vibrations** so small they are imperceptible to humans, even from thousands of **kilometers** away.
 
• These instruments are critical for **disaster management**, **early warning systems**, and scientific research into the **internal structure** of the **Earth**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tiltmeter**:

 
 
• It is an extremely sensitive **inclinometer** used to measure very small changes in the **vertical level** or **slope** of the ground or a structure.
 
• **Uses**: It is primarily used in **volcanology** to monitor the "breathing" or swelling of volcanoes caused by **magma** movement, as well as in **civil engineering** to monitor the stability of **dams** and **tunnels**.
 
 
 
• **Anemometer**:
 
 
• An **anemometer** is a device used for measuring **wind speed** and **wind direction**.
 
• The **cup anemometer**, a common **type**, was invented by **John Thomas Romney Robinson** in **1846**.
 
• **Applications**: It is an essential tool in **meteorology**, **aviation**, and for **navigation** at sea.
 
 
 
• **Barometer**:
 
 
• A **barometer** is a scientific instrument used to measure **atmospheric pressure**.
 
• The first **mercury barometer** was invented by **Evangelista Torricelli** in the **year** **1643**.
 
• **Features**: Since **atmospheric pressure** changes with **altitude** and **weather patterns**, it is used for **weather forecasting** and as an **altimeter** in **aircraft**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **magnitude** of an earthquake is often expressed using the **Richter Scale**, developed by **Charles F. Richter** in **1935**. It is a **logarithmic scale** where each whole **number** increase represents a **ten-fold increase** in measured amplitude.
 
• The **intensity** or the actual damage caused by an earthquake is measured using the **Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) Scale**, which uses **Roman numerals** from **I to XII**.
 
• The point inside the **Earth** where the earthquake starts is called the **focus** or **hypocenter**, while the point directly above it on the **surface** is called the **epicenter**.
 
• In **India**, the **Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)** has classified the country into **four seismic zones** (Zone II, III, IV, and V) based on the **seismic hazard** and **geological** data.

questions.question: Which Act introduced uniform reporting standards for banks to the Reserve Bank of India in 2025?

options.text: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The State Bank of India Act, 1955

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025** (introduced as a Bill in **August 2024**) was designed to update and modernize the regulatory environment for the banking sector in **India**.
 
• One of the most significant **features** of this **Act** is the introduction of **uniform reporting standards** for all scheduled commercial banks. Historically, banks reported their **demand and time liabilities** to the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** based on "reporting Fridays."
 
• Under the new provisions, the reporting frequency has been shifted to specific **dates**, namely the **15th** and the **last day of every month**. This ensures that the **data** provided by banks is consistent and easier to reconcile with other financial **indices** and **surveys**. *Hence, the statement regarding the introduction of uniform reporting standards via this Act is correct.*
 
• This **Act** amends several existing laws, including the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934** and the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, to give the **RBI** greater **functions** in supervising the **liquidity** and **statutory reserves** of banks.
 
• The move to **uniform reporting** aims to reduce **data** discrepancies that occurred due to the variations in the **number** of Fridays in different **months** or **years**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**:

 
 
• This **Act** provided the legal framework for the establishment of the **Reserve Bank of India** on **April 1, 1935**.
 
• It defines the **functions** of the **RBI** as the **country’s** central bank, including the issuance of **currency** notes and the regulation of the **monetary system** to maintain stability in **India**.
 
• It also contains provisions for the **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** that banks must maintain with the **RBI**.
 
 
 
• **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**:
 
 
• Originally passed as the **Banking Companies Act, 1949**, it was later renamed in **1966**.
 
• This **Act** gives the **RBI** the power to **license** banks, regulate their shareholding, and supervise the **appointment** of boards and management.
 
• It applies to both commercial and **cooperative banks** across the **country**, ensuring a safe **banking** environment for depositors.
 
 
 
• **State Bank of India Act, 1955**:
 
 
• This **Act** led to the formation of the **State Bank of India (SBI)** on **July 1, 1955**, by taking over the **Imperial Bank of India**.
 
• Its primary **application** was to expand **banking** facilities in **rural** areas and serve the **government's** financial needs.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Nomination Updates**: The **Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025** increased the **number** of permitted **nominees** per account from **one** to **four**, allowing for **simultaneous** or **successive** nominations.
 
• **Substantial Interest**: The **Act** revised the **numerical value** defining "substantial interest" for directors, increasing it from **Rs. 5 lakhs** to **Rs. 2 crores**, which reflects current **economic data** and **market** valuations.
 
• **Director Tenures**: In the context of **Cooperative Banks**, the **Act** extends the **tenure** of directors to align with other **government guidelines** and laws, specifically moving the **limit** from **eight years** to **ten years** in certain **organizations**.
 
• **Regulatory Reporting**: By shifting to a **fixed-date** reporting system (the **15th** and **30th/31st**), the **RBI** can better calculate the **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** and **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** for the entire **banking** sector simultaneously.

questions.question: Which 17th-century CE monument in Agra, built by Shah Jahan, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Taj Mahal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Taj Mahal** is an ivory-white marble mausoleum located on the southern bank of the **Yamuna River** in **Agra**, **Uttar Pradesh**, **India**. It was commissioned in **1632** by the **Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan** to house the tomb of his beloved wife, **Mumtaz Mahal**. ***Hence, this is the correct option.***
 
• The monument was designated as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **1983** for being "the jewel of Muslim art in **India** and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage." It is also considered one of the **New Seven Wonders of the World**.
 
• **Jama Masjid** (Agra) was built by **Shah Jahan** in **1648** and dedicated to his daughter, **Jahanara Begum**. While it is a significant **17th-century** structure in **Agra**, it is not individually listed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in the same capacity as the **Taj Mahal**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Safdarjung Tomb** is located in **New Delhi** and was built in **1754** for **Nawab Safdarjung** during the late **Mughal Empire** era. Since it was built in the **18th century** and is not located in **Agra**, it does not fit the criteria. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Sikandra Tomb** is the final resting place of the **Mughal Emperor Akbar**. It is located in **Agra**, but its construction was completed by his son, **Emperor Jahangir**, in **1613**. It was not built by **Shah Jahan**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Architectural Style**: The **Taj Mahal** is the pinnacle of **Mughal Architecture**, which is a unique blend of **Indian**, **Persian**, and **Islamic** styles. The construction project involved approximately **20,000 artisans** under the guidance of a board of architects led by **Ustad Ahmad Lahauri**.
 
• **Materials and Decoration**: The main structure is constructed of **white marble** sourced from the quarries of **Makrana** in **Rajasthan**. It is famous for its **Pietra Dura** work, which involves inlaying precious and semi-precious stones like **lapis lazuli**, **jade**, **crystal**, and **turquoise** into the marble to create floral and geometric patterns.
 
• **Timeline**: The construction of the mausoleum was essentially completed in **1643**, but work continued on other phases of the project for another **10 years**. The entire complex is believed to have been completed in its entirety in **1653** at a cost estimated at the time to be around **32 million rupees**.
 
• **The Garden (Charbagh)**: The complex is set around a large **300-metre** square **Charbagh** (Mughal garden). The garden uses raised pathways that divide each of the four quarters of the garden into **16** sunken parterres or flowerbeds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Shah Jahan's Reign**: Known as the **Golden Age** of **Mughal Architecture**, **Shah Jahan** (the **fifth** Mughal Emperor) commissioned several famous monuments including the **Red Fort** (Lal Qila) in **Delhi**, the **Jama Masjid** in **Delhi**, and the city of **Shahjahanabad**.
 
• **UNESCO Sites in Agra**: There are three **UNESCO World Heritage Sites** located in or near **Agra**: the **Taj Mahal** (**1983**), the **Agra Fort** (**1983**), and **Fatehpur Sikri** (**1986**).
 
• **Conservation**: To protect the monument from environmental pollution and the yellowing of marble caused by industrial emissions, the **Government of India** established the **Taj Trapezium Zone (TTZ)**. This is a defined area of **10,400 sq km** around the **Taj Mahal** where strict pollution control standards are enforced.
 
• **Mumtaz Mahal**: She was the second wife of **Shah Jahan**. She died in **1631** in **Burhanpur** while giving birth to their **14th child**, **Gauhara Begum**. Her body was eventually moved to the **Taj Mahal** complex once it was ready.

questions.question: A shopkeeper fixes the marked price of an item 160% above its cost price. What percentage of discount on marked price should be allowed to gain 30%?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let CP = 100

MP = 100 + 160% = 260

Required SP for 30% profit = 130

⇒ Discount = 260 − 130 = 130

⇒ Discount % = (130 ÷ 260) × 100 = 50%

**∴ Answer = 50%**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Markup = 160%, Profit = 30%

**Formula Used:**

Profit % = (SP − CP) ÷ CP × 100

**Calculation:**

⇒ Let CP = 100

⇒ MP = 100 + 160% of 100 = 260

⇒ SP = 100 + 30% of 100 = 130

⇒ Discount = MP − SP = 260 − 130 = 130

⇒ Discount % = (130 ÷ 260) × 100

⇒ = 50%

**∴ Final Answer = 50%**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**Markup Concept:** MP = CP × (1 + Markup%)

**Discount Formula:** Discount % = (Discount ÷ MP) × 100

**Exam Insight:** Taking CP = 100 simplifies all percentage-based problems.

questions.question: If A's salary is 113% more than that of B, then by how much percent is B's salary less than that of A (correct to 2 decimal places)?

A = 100 + 113% = 213

A is 113% more than B

Percentage = (Difference ÷ Base) × 100

⇒ Difference = A − B = 213 − 100 = 113

⇒ Required % = (113 ÷ 213) × 100

questions.question: Which Indian Prime Minister among the following was never the Chief Minister of any state of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chandrashekhar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chandrashekhar** served as the **8th Prime Minister** of **India** from **10 November 1990** to **21 June 1991**. He is the only person among the given options who never held the post of **Chief Minister** of any **Indian State** before becoming the **Prime Minister**. *Hence, this option is correct.*
 
• **Morarji Desai** was the **4th Prime Minister** of **India** (**1977–1979**). Prior to this, he served as the **Chief Minister** of the erstwhile **Bombay State** from **1952** to **1956**. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*
 
• **V.P. Singh** (Vishwanath Pratap Singh) served as the **7th Prime Minister** of **India** from **1989** to **1990**. He had previously served as the **Chief Minister** of **Uttar Pradesh** between **1980** and **1982**. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*
 
• **P.V. Narasimha Rao** was the **9th Prime Minister** of **India**, serving from **1991** to **1996**. He held the office of the **Chief Minister** of **Andhra Pradesh** from **1971** to **1973**. *Hence, this option is incorrect.*
 
• **Chandrashekhar** was also known for the unique distinction of becoming the **Prime Minister** without ever holding any prior **Ministerial portfolio** at the **Central** or **State** level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chandrashekhar's Political Career**:

 
 
• He was popularly known as the **"Young Turk"** for his fiery conviction and opposition to the established **Congress** leadership during the **1960s**.
 
• He hailed from the **Ibrahimpatti** village in the **Ballia** district of **Uttar Pradesh** and was a prominent leader of the **Janata Dal (Socialist)**.
 
• His government was a **minority government** supported by the **Indian National Congress** from the outside, which lasted for only **223 days**.
 
 
 
• **Prime Ministers who were Chief Ministers**:
 
 
• A total of **6** individuals have served as both **Chief Minister** and **Prime Minister** of **India**.
 
• These include **Morarji Desai** (**Bombay State**), **Charan Singh** (**Uttar Pradesh**), **V.P. Singh** (**Uttar Pradesh**), **P.V. Narasimha Rao** (**Andhra Pradesh**), **H.D. Deve Gowda** (**Karnataka**), and **Narendra Modi** (**Gujarat**).
 
• **Narendra Modi** is the **14th** and current **Prime Minister**, having served as the **Chief Minister** of **Gujarat** for four terms from **2001** to **2014**.
 
 
 
• **Prime Ministers who were never Chief Ministers**:
 
 
• Several prominent leaders moved directly to the **Union Cabinet** or the **Prime Minister's Office** without being a **Chief Minister**.
 
• This list includes **Jawaharlal Nehru**, **Lal Bahadur Shastri**, **Indira Gandhi**, **Rajiv Gandhi**, **Atal Bihari Vajpayee**, **I.K. Gujral**, and **Manmohan Singh**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Morarji Desai**: He was the first **non-Congress Prime Minister** of **India** and is the only person to receive the highest civilian awards from both **India** (**Bharat Ratna**) and **Pakistan** (**Nishan-e-Pakistan**).
 
• **V.P. Singh**: His tenure is most remembered for the implementation of the **Mandal Commission** report in **1990**, which provided **27% reservation** for **Other Backward Classes (OBCs)** in central government jobs.
 
• **P.V. Narasimha Rao**: He is often called the **"Father of Indian Economic Reforms"** for initiating the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** policies in **1991** alongside then-Finance Minister **Manmohan Singh**.
 
• **Constitutional Provision**: According to **Article 75** of the **Constitution of India**, the **Prime Minister** is appointed by the **President**, and there is no legal requirement for them to have served as a **Chief Minister** or even a **Minister** previously.

questions.question: Two numbers have an HCF of 12 and an LCM of 840. If one of the numbers is 84, then find the other number.

The product of HCF and LCM of two numbers equals the product of the two numbers.

questions.question: Which of the following scholars introduced the concept of human development?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahbub-ul-Haq**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The concept of human development was introduced by **Dr. Mahbub-ul-Haq**, a **Pakistani** economist, in the year **1990**. He described human development as development that enlarges people's choices and improves their lives.
 
• **Dr. Mahbub-ul-Haq** and **Indian** Nobel laureate **Dr. Amartya Sen** worked together to establish the theoretical underpinnings of the **Human Development Index (HDI)**. While **Dr. Haq** emphasized the expansion of choices, **Dr. Sen** introduced the **"Capability Approach"**, focusing on what people are effectively able to do and be.
 
• According to the concept, the basic goal of development is to create an environment where people can enjoy long, healthy, and creative lives. This shifted the focus of development from purely **economic growth** (measured by **GDP**) to a **people-centric** approach.
 
• The first **Human Development Report (HDR)** was published by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** in **1990**, based on the framework provided by these scholars.
 
• The concept highlights that **income** is not the end-goal of development; rather, it is a means to achieve human development. The real wealth of a nation is its people.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Alexander Von Humboldt**: He was a **Prussian** polymath, geographer, and naturalist who lived from **1769 to 1859**. He is widely recognized as the **"Father of Modern Geography"**. His work, **"Cosmos"**, attempted to unify various branches of scientific knowledge and culture.
 
• **Amartya Sen**: An **Indian** economist and philosopher who was awarded the **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences** in **1998**. His contribution to **welfare economics** and social choice theory has been monumental, particularly his work on **famines** and the **human development** framework.
 
• **Griffith Taylor**: An **Australian** geographer who introduced the concept of **Neo-determinism**, also known as **"Stop and Go Determinism"**. This theory suggests that humans can accelerate, slow, or stop the speed of a country's development, but they should not depart from the main trends set by the **environment**.
 
• **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)**: Established in **1965**, it is the **UN's** global development network. It helps countries eliminate **poverty** and achieve sustainable human development. It has been publishing the **Human Development Report** annually since **1990**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Human Development Index (HDI)** is a composite index that measures average achievement in **three** basic dimensions of human development:

 
 
• **Health**: Measured by **Life Expectancy at Birth**.
 
• **Education**: Measured by **Mean Years of Schooling** for adults aged **25 years** and more and **Expected Years of Schooling** for children of school-entering age.
 
• **Standard of Living**: Measured by **Gross National Income (GNI) per capita** (at **Purchasing Power Parity** in **US Dollars**).
 
 
 
• The **HDI** value ranges from **0 to 1**. Countries are categorized into four tiers: **Very High**, **High**, **Medium**, and **Low** human development.
 
• In recent reports, **Norway**, **Switzerland**, and **Iceland** often rank at the top of the **HDI** list, reflecting high investment in **social infrastructure** and **public health**.
 
• Other indices related to human development include the **Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI)**, the **Gender Development Index (GDI)**, and the **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Inertia** is defined as the inherent property of a body by virtue of which it resists any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line. It is the natural tendency of objects to resist changes in their state of motion. ***Hence, the correct answer is Inertia.***
 
• **Acceleration** is the rate of change of **velocity** of an object with respect to **time**. It occurs only when an external **unbalanced force** acts on an object. It describes how the motion changes rather than the tendency to remain undisturbed. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Momentum** is a **vector quantity** defined as the product of the **mass** and **velocity** of an object ($p = mv$). It represents the "quantity of motion" possessed by a moving body and depends on how much stuff is moving and how fast it is moving. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Force** is an external agent (push or pull) capable of changing the state of rest or motion of a particular body. It has a **magnitude** and a **direction**, making it a **vector quantity**. While force causes motion, **Inertia** is the resistance to that motion. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• The relationship between these concepts is governed by **Newton’s Laws of Motion**, where **Inertia** relates to the first law, and **Force**, **Mass**, and **Acceleration** relate to the second law ($F = ma$).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's First Law of Motion**: Also known as the **Law of Inertia**, it states that an object will remain at rest or move in a straight line with constant **velocity** unless it is acted upon by an external **force**. This law was built upon the earlier ideas of **Galileo Galilei**.
 
• **Measurement of Inertia**: The **mass** of an object is a **quantitative measure** of its inertia. The larger the **mass** of a body, the greater is its **inertia**. For example, a heavy stone has more inertia than a small ball, meaning it requires more **force** to change its state. The **SI unit** of mass is the **kilogram (kg)**.
 
• **Types of Inertia**:
 
 
• **Inertia of Rest**: The inability of a body to change its state of rest by itself. Example: When a bus starts suddenly, the passengers lean backwards.
 
• **Inertia of Motion**: The inability of a body to change its state of uniform motion by itself. Example: An athlete runs some distance before taking a long jump to gain momentum.
 
• **Inertia of Direction**: The inability of a body to change its direction of motion by itself. Example: When a car takes a sharp turn, passengers are thrown to the outer side.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context**: Before the **17th century**, it was believed that the "natural state" of objects was to be at rest. It was **Galileo** who first suggested that in the absence of **friction**, an object would keep moving forever, a concept **Isaac Newton** later formalized in **1687** in his work "**Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Relationship with Gravity**: While **Inertia** depends solely on **mass**, weight depends on the **gravitational pull**. An object has the same **inertia** on the **Earth** as it does on the **Moon**, even though its weight changes.
 
• **Applications**: **Inertia** is the reason why **seatbelts** are mandatory in vehicles. When a car stops abruptly due to **brakes**, the passenger's body continues to move forward due to the **Inertia of Motion**. The seatbelt provides the external **force** to stop the body safely.
 
• **Mathematical Representation**: Though **Inertia** doesn't have a specific formula like **Force**, it is proportional to **Mass** ($I \propto m$). In rotational mechanics, this concept is called the **Moment of Inertia**, which depends on the distribution of mass relative to the axis of rotation.

questions.question: What does the crude birth rate (CBR) measure in demographic studies?

options.text: Number of live births per thousand annually
Ratio of deaths per hundred population
Share of employed women in workforce

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Number of live births per thousand annually**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)** is defined as the number of **live births** occurring among the population of a given geographical area during a given **year**, per **1,000** mid-year total population of the given area during the same year.
 
• It is called **"crude"** because it does not take into account the **age or gender** composition of the population, specifically the proportion of women in the **reproductive age group**.
 
• **Statement 1:** Net rural to urban migration refers to the movement of people from countryside areas to cities to seek better **employment** or living conditions, which is a measure of **urbanization**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement 2:** The **Crude Birth Rate** specifically measures the frequency of **live births** in a population per **1,000** individuals annually. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• **Statement 3:** The ratio of deaths per population is measured by the **Crude Death Rate (CDR)**, which is also calculated per **1,000** individuals, not per hundred. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **Statement 4:** The share of employed women in the workforce is a **socio-economic indicator** known as the **Female Labour Force Participation Rate (FLFPR)**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Global and National Context:** The **Crude Birth Rate** varies significantly across different countries. **Developing nations**, particularly in **Sub-Saharan Africa**, often exhibit high CBRs (frequently above **30 per 1,000**), while **developed countries** in **Europe** and **East Asia** (like **Japan** and **Germany**) have CBRs below **10 per 1,000**.
 
• **Indian Demographic Data:** In **India**, the **Sample Registration System (SRS)** is the primary source of **CBR** data. As per recent reports, the CBR in India has seen a steady **decline** due to increased **literacy**, **urbanization**, and **family planning** initiatives. For example, states like **Bihar** have historically recorded higher birth rates, whereas **Kerala** and **Tamil Nadu** record much lower rates.
 
• **Significance:** CBR is a crucial metric for **demographers** and **policymakers** as it helps in **population projections** and the planning of **maternal and child health services**. It is one of the primary components used to calculate the **Natural Increase** of a population (CBR minus CDR).
 
• **Applications:** Governments use this data to allocate **resources** for **education**, **healthcare**, and **infrastructure**. A high CBR suggests a **younger population** structure, while a low CBR indicates an **ageing population**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Calculation Formula:** The CBR is calculated as **(Total Number of Live Births / Total Mid-year Population) × 1,000**. The mid-year population is used to represent the average population over the **year**.
 
• **Difference from Fertility Rates:** Unlike the **General Fertility Rate (GFR)** or **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)**, which focus specifically on women in the **childbearing age** (usually **15–49 years**), the CBR includes the **entire population** (men, children, and the elderly) in its denominator.
 
• **Influencing Factors:** Factors that affect the CBR include the **average age of marriage**, availability of **contraception**, **cultural norms** regarding family size, and the level of **economic development**.
 
• **Relation to SDGs:** Monitoring birth rates and reproductive health is integral to achieving **United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-being)** and **Goal 5 (Gender Equality)**.

questions.question: Which of the following three river systems are primarily responsible for the formation of the Northern Plains of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Northern Plains** of **India** are formed by the interplay of three major river systems: the **Indus**, the **Ganga**, and the **Brahmaputra**, along with their numerous **tributaries**.
 
• This vast plain is composed of **alluvial soil**, which was deposited over **millions of years** in a large basin located at the foothills of the **Himalayas**.
 
• Geographically, the plains extend over an area of approximately **7 lakh square kilometers**. The plain is about **2,400 km long** and ranges between **240 to 320 km in width**.
 
• It is a **densely populated** physiographic division due to the combination of a **rich soil cover**, **adequate water supply**, and a **favorable climate**, making it the most **agriculturally productive** part of **India**.
 
• The rivers flowing from the **northern mountains** are involved in **depositional work**. In their lower courses, due to a gentle slope, the velocity of the river decreases, leading to the formation of **riverine islands** and **distributaries**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indus River System:**

 
 
• The **Indus** originates in **Tibet** near **Lake Mansarovar**. It flows west and enters **India** in the **Ladakh** district.
 
• Its main tributaries in **India** are the **Zanskar**, **Nubra**, **Shyok**, and **Hunza**. In the **Punjab** region, the **Jhelum**, **Chenab**, **Ravi**, **Beas**, and **Satluj** join the **Indus**.
 
• The western part of the Northern Plain is referred to as the **Punjab Plains**, dominated by **doabs** (land between two rivers).
 
 
 
• **Ganga River System:**
 
 
• The **Ganga** is formed by the confluence of the **Alaknanda** and **Bhagirathi** at **Devprayag**. It has a total length of **2,525 km**.
 
• The **Ganga Plain** extends between the **Ghaggar** and **Teesta** rivers. It spreads over the states of **Haryana**, **Delhi**, **Uttar Pradesh**, **Bihar**, and parts of **Jharkhand** and **West Bengal**.
 
• Major tributaries include the **Yamuna**, **Ghaghara**, **Gandak**, and **Kosi**.
 
 
 
• **Brahmaputra River System:**
 
 
• The **Brahmaputra** rises in **Tibet** (where it is known as the **Tsangpo**), east of **Mansarovar lake**.
 
• It enters **India** through a gorge in **Arunachal Pradesh** (as the **Dihang**) and flows through **Assam**, where it forms the **Brahmaputra Valley**.
 
• It is known for having the **world's largest riverine island**, **Majuli**, located in the state of **Assam**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Northern Plains** are generally divided into four regions based on relief features:

 
 
• **Bhabar:** A narrow belt of **8 to 16 km** in width consisting of **pebbles** where rivers disappear underground.
 
• **Terai:** A **marshy and swampy** region south of the Bhabar, characterized by **thick forests** and **wildlife**.
 
• **Bhangar:** The **older alluvium** of the plains, forming a **terrace-like feature** above the floodplains, often containing **calcareous deposits** known as **Kankar**.
 
• **Khadar:** The **newer, younger deposits** of the floodplains that are **renewed almost every year**, making them ideal for **intensive agriculture**.
 
 
 
• The **Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta**, also known as the **Sundarbans**, is the **largest delta in the world** and is famous for **Royal Bengal Tigers** and **mangrove forests**.

questions.question: Which treaty was signed on 17 July 2025 between the United Kingdom and Germany, marking their first bilateral treaty since the Second World War?

• **Trade and investment**

questions.question: According to the 2025 Human Development Report, what was India’s Human Development Index (HDI) value for the year 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.644**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **Human Development Report 2023-24** (released in **March 2024**), which provides the latest data for the **2022-2023** period, India’s **Human Development Index (HDI)** value increased to **0.644**.
 
• India’s global rank stands at **134th** out of **193** countries and territories surveyed in the latest report.
 
• The report indicates a significant recovery from the **COVID-19 pandemic** period, as India’s HDI value was **0.633** in **2021** and **0.642** in **2020**.
 
• India is classified under the **Medium Human Development** category, showing consistent progress in life expectancy and education metrics over the past decade.
 
• The **HDI** is a composite index that measures average achievement in three basic dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dimensions and Indicators:**

 
 
• **Life Expectancy:** India’s life expectancy at birth improved to **67.7 years** in **2022**, up from **67.2 years** in **2021**.
 
• **Education:** The **Expected Years of Schooling (EYS)** for India is **12.6 years**, while the **Mean Years of Schooling (MYS)** is **6.57 years**.
 
• **Economic Standard:** India's **Gross National Income (GNI) per capita** (at 2017 PPP prices) is reported at **$6,951**.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• The **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** has been publishing the **Human Development Report (HDR)** annually since **1990**.
 
• The concept of HDI was developed by Pakistani economist **Mahbub ul Haq** and Indian Nobel laureate **Amartya Sen**.
 
• **Switzerland**, **Norway**, and **Iceland** consistently rank at the top of the global HDI list.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Gender Inequality Index (GII):** India has also shown improvement in the **GII**, ranking **108th** out of 193 countries with a value of **0.437**, which is better than the global average.
 
• **Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI):** When adjusted for inequality, India’s HDI value falls, highlighting the disparity in the distribution of development across the population. India’s **IHDI** value for **2022** was approximately **0.434**.
 
• **Planetary Pressures:** Recent reports also include the **Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI)**, which accounts for carbon dioxide emissions and material footprint per capita to reflect sustainable development.

questions.question: Select the INCORRECT statement about the polices of Jalaluddin Khalji.

options.text: He avoided harsh punishments, even to those who revolted against him.
He put forward the view that the state should never be based on the willing support of the governed.
He tried to win the goodwill of the nobility by a policy of tolerance.
He not only forgave those who revolted against him but at times even rewarded them to win their support.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**He put forward the view that the state should never be based on the willing support of the governed**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jalaluddin Khalji**, who ascended the throne in **1290 AD**, was the first sultan of the **Delhi Sultanate** to clearly put forward the view that the state should be based on the **willing support** of the governed. He believed that since the large majority of the people in **India** were **Hindus**, the state in India could not be a truly **Islamic state**. *Hence, the statement that he believed the state should "never" be based on willing support is incorrect.*
 
• He was known for his **policy of clemency** and avoided harsh punishments, even toward those who conspired against him. He famously stated that he was an **"old Muslim"** and was not accustomed to shedding the blood of **Muslims**. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*
 
• Upon his accession, **Jalaluddin Khalji** did not eliminate the existing **nobility**. Instead, he tried to win their **goodwill** by allowing many of the old **Balbani nobles** to retain their posts and status, aiming for a peaceful transition of power. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*
 
• A significant example of his **tolerance** was his reaction to the revolt of **Malik Chajju** (a nephew of **Balban**) in **Kara**. After the revolt was suppressed, **Jalaluddin** not only **forgave** the rebels but also hosted a feast for them, praising their loyalty to their former master's family. *Hence, statement 4 is correct.*
 
• His reign marked the beginning of the **Khalji Dynasty** and a shift in the nature of the **Delhi Sultanate**'s administration toward a more **liberal** and less **exclusionary** approach compared to the previous **Ilbari Turks**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Background and Accession:** **Jalaluddin Firuz Khalji** came to power at the **age of 70** after the downfall of the **Mamluk Dynasty**. His rise to the throne is often called the **"Khalji Revolution"** because it ended the monopoly of the **Turkish nobility** and opened high offices to **Indian Muslims** and **Khaljis**.
 
• **The Sidi Maula Incident:** While he was generally **merciful**, the execution of the **Sufi saint Sidi Maula** remains a rare instance of **harshness** during his reign. **Sidi Maula** was accused of plotting a **rebellion** and was eventually trampled by an **elephant**.
 
• **Mongol Invasion:** In **1292 AD**, a **Mongol** army led by **Abdullah** (grandson of **Hulagu Khan**) invaded **India**. **Jalaluddin** successfully repelled the invasion. He allowed many **Mongols** to settle near **Delhi** after they converted to **Islam**; these settlers became known as **"New Muslims"**.
 
• **Internal Challenges:** His **mild policies** were often criticized by the younger **Khalji officers**, including his nephew **Alauddin Khalji**, who viewed his **tolerance** as a sign of **weakness** that encouraged **lawlessness**.
 
• **End of Reign:** His reign ended in **July 1296** when he was **assassinated** by his nephew and son-in-law, **Alauddin Khalji**, during a meeting at **Kara-Manikpur**. This act led to **Alauddin Khalji** becoming the next **Sultan**, who shifted the state back to a policy of **harsh discipline** and **centralization**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Administrative Philosophy:** Unlike **Balban**, who believed in the **"Theory of Divine Right"** and maintained a **rigid** distance from the common people, **Jalaluddin** sought to humanize the **monarchy**.
 
• **Geographical Reach:** During his short reign, he attempted expeditions to **Ranthambore** in **1291 AD** but retreated to avoid the **loss of Muslim lives**, further demonstrating his **non-violent** inclinations toward his co-religionists.
 
• **Legacy:** Though his **lenient** approach was short-lived, it set a precedent for **secular considerations** in **Indian governance**, emphasizing that a ruler must account for the **demographics** and **sentiments** of the **population**.

questions.question: Which characteristic of computers enables them to perform various tasks such as calculations, graphics, and communication?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Versatility**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Versatility** is one of the most significant characteristics of a computer, referring to its capacity to perform **completely different types of work** at the same time or in rapid succession. This allows a single machine to transition from **complex mathematical calculations** to **multimedia processing**, **graphic design**, or **global communication** effortlessly.
 
• This characteristic is fundamentally rooted in the **programmability** of the computer. Unlike a calculator or a dedicated machine that can only perform specific functions, a computer's **hardware** is designed to follow any set of **logical instructions** provided via **software applications**.
 
• In a professional environment, **Versatility** enables a user to use a computer for **preparing a spreadsheet**, then switch to **editing a high-resolution video**, and simultaneously manage **emails** or **web browsing**. This multi-functional nature makes it an essential tool in every **modern industry**.
 
• The **versatile** nature of computers is categorized by the ability to handle both **numerical data** and **non-numerical data** (like text, sound, and images), making them **universal machines**. Hence, the statement that versatility allows for various tasks is correct.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Speed**: Computers are high-speed **electronic devices** capable of performing millions of **calculations** per second. The speed of a **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** is typically measured in **Hertz (Hz)**, with modern processors operating in the **Gigahertz (GHz)** range. This allows tasks that would take humans years to be completed in **microseconds** or **nanoseconds**.
 
• **Accuracy**: Computers are known for their extreme **precision**. As long as the **input data** and the **program instructions** are correct, the computer will produce error-free results. Errors in computing are usually the result of **human error**, often referred to as **GIGO (Garbage In, Garbage Out)**.
 
• **Automation**: Once a **program** or a set of **instructions** is loaded into the **computer memory**, the machine can execute the task **automatically** without human intervention. This feature is critical in **manufacturing**, **robotics**, and **large-scale data processing**.
 
• **Diligence**: Unlike human beings, a computer is free from **tiredness**, **monotony**, and **lack of concentration**. It can work for hours or even days performing the exact same **repetitive task** with the same **speed** and **accuracy** as the first time.
 
• **Storage Capacity**: Computers have the ability to store enormous amounts of **information** in very small physical spaces. Data can be stored in **Primary Memory (RAM)** for immediate use or in **Secondary Storage** like **Hard Disk Drives (HDD)**, **Solid State Drives (SSD)**, and **Cloud Storage** for long-term retrieval.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **History and Evolution**: The concept of a **versatile** computer was first envisioned by **Charles Babbage** with his **Analytical Engine** in the **19th Century**. Since then, the transition from **vacuum tubes** to **transistors** and finally to **Integrated Circuits (ICs)** has exponentially increased the **functional range** of computers.
 
• **Modern Applications**: Today, the **versatility** of computers is seen in **Artificial Intelligence (AI)**, **Machine Learning**, and **Internet of Things (IoT)**, where computers are integrated into **smart homes**, **autonomous vehicles**, and **medical diagnostic tools**.
 
• **Logical Power**: A computer is a **logical machine**. Its **Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)** allows it to make **comparisons** and **decisions** based on **binary logic** (0s and 1s), which is the foundation of all its complex **operations**.

questions.question: Two trains are running with the speed of 49 km/hr and 59 km/hr towards each other on parallel tracks. Their lengths are 349 m and 371 m, respectively. In how much time (in seconds) will they completely pass each other?

Opposite direction ⇒ Relative speed = 49 + 59 = 108 km/hr

⇒ Convert to m/s: 108 × 5/18 = 30 m/s

Total distance = 349 + 371 = 720 m

questions.question: Which landform is formed when a glacier erodes a pre-existing river valley by widening, deepening, and smoothing it?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**U-shaped valley**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **U-shaped valley**, also known as a **glacial trough**, is formed when a **glacier** travels across and down a slope, carving the valley through the action of **scouring**.
 
• Glaciers typically follow the path of **pre-existing river valleys**. While rivers create **V-shaped valleys** through **vertical erosion**, glaciers transform them by **widening**, **deepening**, and **smoothing** the landscape.
 
• The process involves massive **ice sheets** or **alpine glaciers** that exert immense pressure on the valley floor and walls. This leads to the removal of **interlocking spurs**, resulting in a **straightened** and **broadened** valley.
 
• These valleys are characterized by **steep, nearly vertical side walls** and a **wide, flat valley floor**. When these valleys are filled with **seawater** after the glacier melts, they are referred to as **fjords**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the U-shaped valley is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **V-shaped valley**:

 
 
• These are formed by the **erosional action** of **rivers** in their **youthful stage**.
 
• The **river** cuts **downward** into the **bedrock** more rapidly than the **valley sides** are eroded, resulting in a **narrow** and **deep** shape resembling the letter **'V'**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect as it relates to river erosion, not glacial.***
 
 
 
• **Gorge**:
 
 
• A **gorge** is a **narrow valley** with **steep, rocky walls** located between **hills** or **mountains**.
 
• It is often formed by **rivers** or **geological shifts** over **millions of years**. A famous example is the **Grand Canyon** in the **United States**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect as it describes a narrow, deep river-cut feature.***
 
 
 
• **Floodplain**:
 
 
• A **floodplain** is a **flat area of land** next to a **river** or **stream**.
 
• It stretches from the **banks** of the **river** to the outer **edges** of the **valley**. It is a **depositional landform** composed of **alluvium** (silt, sand, and clay) deposited during **floods**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect as it is a depositional river landform.***
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mechanisms of Glacial Erosion**:

 
 
• **Plucking**: This occurs when **meltwater** freezes into **cracks** in the **rock**; as the **glacier** moves, it pulls out **large chunks** of **stone**.
 
• **Abrasion**: The **debris** frozen into the **ice** acts like **sandpaper**, **grinding** and **polishing** the **valley floor** and **walls** as the **glacier** slides.
 
 
 
• **Geological Timeline**: Most prominent **U-shaped valleys** were formed during the **Pleistocene Epoch** (approximately **2.6 million** to **11,700 years** ago) when **glaciation** was widespread across the **Northern Hemisphere**.
 
• **Global Examples**:
 
 
• **Yosemite Valley** in **California, USA**, is a world-renowned **U-shaped valley**.
 
• The **Lauterbrunnen Valley** in **Switzerland** features **72 waterfalls** plunging over **vertical glacial walls**.
 
• In **India**, the **Leh-Ladakh** region and parts of the **Himalayas** exhibit classic **glacial topography**.
 
 
 
• **Associated Features**: Often found with **hanging valleys** (smaller valleys left high above the main floor), **cirques** (bowl-shaped depressions), and **moraines** (accumulations of dirt and rocks).

questions.question: A boat covers a certain distance downstream in 6 hours and takes 8 hours to return upstream to the starting point. If the speed of the stream is 4 km/h, find the speed of the boat in still water.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let boat speed = x

Downstream speed = x + 4, Upstream speed = x − 4

Same distance ⇒ ratio of speeds = inverse of time

⇒ (x + 4) : (x − 4) = 8 : 6 = 4 : 3

⇒ 3(x + 4) = 4(x − 4)

⇒ 3x + 12 = 4x − 16 ⇒ x = 28

**∴ Answer = 28 km/h**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Downstream time = 6 hr, Upstream time = 8 hr

Speed of stream = 4 km/hr

**Formula Used:**

Speed = Distance ÷ Time

**Calculation:**

⇒ Let distance = D

⇒ Downstream speed = D ÷ 6

⇒ Upstream speed = D ÷ 8

⇒ Boat speed = (Downstream + Upstream) ÷ 2

⇒ = (D/6 + D/8) ÷ 2

⇒ = (4D + 3D) ÷ 24 × 1/2

⇒ = 7D ÷ 48

⇒ Stream speed = (Downstream − Upstream) ÷ 2

⇒ 4 = (D/6 − D/8) ÷ 2

⇒ 4 = (4D − 3D) ÷ 24 × 1/2

⇒ 4 = D ÷ 48

⇒ D = 192

⇒ Boat speed = 7D ÷ 48 = 7 × 192 ÷ 48 = 28 km/hr

**∴ Final Answer = 28 km/h**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

**Stream Formula:** Stream speed = (Downstream − Upstream) ÷ 2

Triangle OAB is right-angled

Radius is perpendicular to tangent at point of contact

⇒ 6² = 3² + AB²

⇒ 36 = 9 + AB²

⇒ AB = √27

⇒ cos∠OBA = OB/OA = 3/6 = 1/2

⇒ ∠OBA = 60°

⇒ Since AB = AC, symmetry gives ∠OBC = 30°

questions.question: Which launch vehicle was announced in 2025 as having been built entirely by the private sector for the first time in India and was set to place the Oceansat satellite into orbit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV)** is the first Indian launch vehicle to be entirely manufactured by the **private sector** through a consortium. This transition marks a significant milestone in India's space reforms initiated in **2020**.
 
• A consortium consisting of **Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL)** and **Larsen & Toubro (L&T)** was awarded the contract by **NewSpace India Limited (NSIL)** to produce five **PSLV** rockets. This was the first time an entire launch vehicle was outsourced to domestic industry.
 
• The mission set for **2025** involving the **Oceansat** series (specifically **EOS-06/Oceansat-3** follow-on missions) is designed to be executed using these privately manufactured rockets. **Oceansat** satellites are intended for oceanographic studies and are typically placed in a **Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit** at an altitude of about **720 km**.
 
• The **PSLV** is famously known as the **"Workhorse of ISRO"** due to its high success rate and versatility. It has four stages, using a combination of **solid and liquid propellants**.
 
• The shift to private manufacturing allows **ISRO** to focus more on **Research and Development (R&D)** and deep-space exploration missions, while the commercial arm handles routine satellite launches.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Launch Vehicle Mark-3 (LVM3):**

 
 
• Formerly known as **GSLV Mk-III**, it is India’s heaviest launch vehicle. It is a **three-stage** vehicle with two solid strap-on motors, a liquid core stage, and a **cryogenic upper stage**.
 
• It is capable of carrying up to **4,000 kg** to **Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO)** and **8,000 kg** to **Low Earth Orbit (LEO)**. It was recently used for the **Chandrayaan-3** mission and **OneWeb** satellite launches.
 
 
 
• **Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV):**
 
 
• This vehicle is specifically designed to place communication satellites into **Geosynchronous orbits**. It features the **Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS)**.
 
• It has a lift-off mass of approximately **414 tonnes** and is essential for India's **INSAT** and **GSAT** series of satellites.
 
 
 
• **Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV):**
 
 
• The **SSLV** is a **three-stage** all-solid vehicle designed to cater to the "launch-on-demand" market for **mini, micro, and nano satellites** (up to **500 kg**).
 
• It offers a **low-cost**, rapid turnaround time and requires **minimal launch infrastructure** compared to larger rockets.
 
 
 
• **Oceansat Satellite Series:**
 
 
• The **Oceansat** satellites carry instruments like the **Ocean Colour Monitor (OCM)** and **Scatterometer**.
 
• These tools provide crucial **data** on chlorophyll concentration, phytoplankton blooms, and **oceanic surface wind vectors**, which are used for **fishery forecasting** and **weather monitoring**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **NSIL (NewSpace India Limited):** It is a **Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE)** under the **Department of Space (DoS)**, established in **2019**. Its primary mandate is to commercially exploit the R&D work of **ISRO**.
 
• **IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre):** It acts as a **single-window**, independent nodal agency to promote and authorize **private sector participation** in the space domain.
 
• **PSLV History:** The first successful launch of **PSLV** took place in **October 1994** (PSLV-D2). Since then, it has launched iconic missions like **Chandrayaan-1 (2008)** and the **Mars Orbiter Mission (2013)**.

questions.question: Why is RAM called “Random Access”?

options.text: Data is stored randomly without structure
Data can be accessed directly from any location
Data can only be accessed sequentially

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Data can be accessed directly from any location**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Random Access Memory (RAM)** is referred to as "Random Access" because any **storage location**, also known as a **memory address**, can be accessed directly by the **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** without having to go through a sequence of other locations. This statement is **correct**.
 
• The term "Random" implies that the **time** taken to access any specific **byte** of data is **constant**, regardless of where it is physically located on the **silicon chip**. This is a primary feature of **main memory** in modern computers.
 
• In contrast to **Sequential Access** media, such as **magnetic tapes** or older **cassettes**, where the system must read through data linearly to reach a specific point, RAM allows for **instantaneous retrieval** of data. This statement is **correct**.
 
• The **memory controller** uses a **binary address** sent by the CPU to locate data in a **grid-like structure** consisting of **rows and columns**. By identifying the **intersection** of a specific row and column, the system retrieves the **data bit** immediately.
 
• RAM acts as a **high-speed temporary workspace** for the **operating system** and **applications**. It stores the data that the CPU is currently processing to ensure **system performance** remains fluid. This statement is **correct**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Volatility:** One of the most critical characteristics of RAM is that it is **volatile memory**. This means that all stored **information** is erased immediately when the **power source** is disconnected or the computer is **restarted**.
 
• **Types of RAM:** There are two main categories: **SRAM (Static RAM)** and **DRAM (Dynamic RAM)**. **SRAM** is faster and used for **CPU Cache**, while **DRAM** is more common, less expensive, and used for the **main system memory**.
 
• **Evolution and Standards:** Over the years, RAM has evolved through various standards like **SDRAM**, **DDR (Double Data Rate)**, **DDR2**, **DDR3**, **DDR4**, and the latest **DDR5**, which was introduced around **2020** to provide higher **bandwidth** and lower **power consumption**.
 
• **Capacity and Measurement:** RAM capacity is measured in **Gigabytes (GB)** in modern computing. Common configurations for **laptops** and **desktops** in **2024** range from **8 GB** to **64 GB**, depending on the **application** (e.g., gaming, video editing, or general use).
 
• **Historical Context:** The first form of **magnetic-core memory** was developed in the late **1940s**, but the modern **MOS (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor)** RAM chip was pioneered by **Robert Dennard** at **IBM** in **1966**, revolutionizing how **data** is handled in **integrated circuits**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Function in Multitasking:** The amount of RAM determines how many **applications** a computer can run simultaneously. If the RAM is full, the operating system uses **Virtual Memory** (a portion of the **Hard Drive** or **SSD**), which significantly **slows down** the computer.
 
• **Read/Write Capabilities:** Unlike **ROM (Read-Only Memory)**, which is generally used for **firmware** and cannot be easily modified, RAM allows for both **reading** and **writing** of data at extremely high **frequencies**.
 
• **Latency:** While RAM is extremely fast, it still has **latency**, which is the **delay** between the **request** for data and the **delivery** of that data to the CPU. Lower latency results in a more **responsive system**.
 
• **Location:** RAM modules, often called **DIMMs (Dual In-line Memory Modules)**, are located in **slots** on the **motherboard**, allowing for easy **upgrades** in most **desktop computers**.

questions.question: If 9 students can prepare 117 charts in 3 hours, how many students are needed to prepare 208 charts in 1 hour?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

⇒ 9 students in 3 hr → 117 charts

⇒ 1 student in 1 hr → 117 ÷ (9 × 3) = 117/27 = 13/3

⇒ Required students for 208 charts in 1 hr:

⇒ x × (13/3) = 208

⇒ x = 208 × 3 ÷ 13 = 48

**∴ Answer = 48**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**
